newsitem.title: MOLDOVA: MOLDOVA EXPECTS TO RESTORE GROWTH IN 1997.
newsitem.headline: MOLDOVA EXPECTS TO RESTORE GROWTH IN 1997.

text.p: Moldovan government expects 1997 to become the first year of economic growth after five years of recession, a senior government official said.
"Our primary goal for the next year is to maintain macroeconomic stabilization and to restore growth," Ion Gutu, Moldovan Deputy Prime Minister, told a news conference on Wednesday.

Gutu disclosed the programme of the new Moldovan government, formed after the December presidential elections. The government has only one year at its disposal, as it has to resign after the next parliamentary elections, due in February 1998.
International financial organizations praised Moldova for its reforms record, saying that it remains within the first group of former Soviet countries in terms of macroeconomic stabilization.
The national currency, Moldovan leu, remained stable since its introduction in 1993, and inflation was supressed from 105 percent in 1994 to 15.1 percent last year.
But in terms of structural reforms Moldova is substantially behind the Baltic states, foreign donors say.
"We did not fulfilled all the masures, agreed upon with the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank," Gutu said.
In 1996 the government failed to stop the decline. Instead of expected growth, the GDP dropped by 8 percent. The budget deficit also was 8 percent instead of the planned 3.5 percent.

The new government set ambitious targets for 1997, planning to increase the GDP by 5-7 percent, industrial production by 11 percent, agriculture by 6.3 percent, exports by 5 percent and to attract 700 million lei of capital investment.
The programme stipulates for further reduction of inflation to 10-13 percent, narrowing the budget deficit to 3 percent and increasing the average monthly salary to 215 lei from 180 lei in 1996.
Gutu called 'urgent tasks' clearing of pension and salaries arrears, which stay at 400 million lei, and curbing crime and corruption.

The government intends to turn from mass vaucher-scheme privatisation to cash privatisation, in particular, of the energy sector and telecommunications. It will present to the parliament laws, which would allow to sell, buy and mortgage the land.
Gutu said the government would have to introduce some unpopular measures to stop production losses.

This week, bread prices in Moldova were increased by 17 percent. By the end of the year, the government intends to increase the energy tariffs by 35 percent for phisical persons and by 10-15 percent for economic agents.

In an attempt to reform the pension system, the government elaborated a draft law on increasing the pension age from 55 to 60 years for women and from 60 to 65 years for men. But the trade unions and the parliament oppose that legislation.
